glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Jesus closes the Sermon on the Mount by calling His hearers to examine themselves, to trust their good Father, and to act on His words, because only a life built on hearing and doing them will stand when the storm comes, a picture that points especially to the coming judgment.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: After Jesus’ ministry throughout Galilee drew great multitudes (4:23–25), He went up on a mountain and taught His disciples (5:1–2). Matthew 7 completes that teaching, and its last verses show the crowds listening as well.

glance.label: Chapter Outline

  • Matthew 7:7–12 — Ask, Seek, Knock, and the Golden Rule

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “Therefore whoever hears these sayings of Mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man who built his house on the rock” (Matthew 7:24).

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Matthew 7 gathers up the Sermon on the Mount and presses it toward a decision. The first half still teaches how disciples live with one another before God. Jesus forbids the judging that fixes on a speck in a brother’s eye while ignoring the plank in one’s own, yet He keeps discernment in place when holy things are met with contempt (7:1–6). He then turns His hearers toward a Father who will “give good things to those who ask Him” (7:11), and out of that generosity comes the call to do for others what we would want done for us (7:12).

From 7:13 onward Jesus sets two gates, two kinds of trees, and two builders before His listeners, and each pair separates appearance from reality. Sheep’s clothing can hide a wolf (7:15). Between the trees and the builders stands a distinct warning: “Lord, Lord” (7:21) can come from people who claim great works in His name, yet Jesus says He never knew them (7:23), because they did not do the Father’s will. The two builders then both hear His sayings, but only one does them, and the storm, which points especially to final judgment, reveals the difference (7:24–27). Jesus also places Himself at the center of that decision. He is the One people will face “in that day,” and His own sayings are the rock on which a life must be built (7:22, 24). Matthew closes by recording that the crowds sensed this authority (7:28–29).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Matthew 7:1–6 — Judging Others and Exercising Discernment

Jesus forbids hypocritical judgment, warning that the measure we use on others will be measured back to us, and tells the one with a plank in his own eye to deal with it first so that he can see clearly to help his brother. He then calls for discernment, since what is holy and precious can be trampled, and the one who offers it attacked, by those who treat it with contempt.

Matthew 7:7–12 — Ask, Seek, Knock, and the Golden Rule

Jesus urges earnest, persevering prayer and grounds it in the Father’s goodness: if earthly fathers give good gifts to their children, the Father in heaven will much more give good things to those who ask Him. Following that teaching, He calls disciples to take the initiative in doing to others what they would want done to them, and He presents this as the sum of the Law and the Prophets.

Matthew 7:13–14 — The Narrow and Wide Gates

Jesus commands His hearers to enter by the narrow gate. The wide gate and broad way carry many toward destruction, while the narrow gate and difficult way lead to life, and the contrast presses each hearer to enter rather than follow the crowd.

Matthew 7:15–20 — Recognizing False Prophets by Their Fruit

Jesus warns of false prophets who look like sheep but inwardly are ravenous wolves. Their fruit, their teaching and conduct themselves, reveals what they truly are, and Jesus warns that every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.

Matthew 7:21–23 — Doing the Father’s Will

Jesus declares that the one who does the will of His Father in heaven will enter the kingdom, and calling Him “Lord, Lord” is not enough. On that day many will claim to have prophesied, cast out demons, and done many wonders in His name, yet He will tell them He never knew them and command them to depart as those who practice lawlessness.

Matthew 7:24–29 — The Wise and Foolish Builders

Jesus pictures two men who hear His sayings: the one who does them builds on the rock and his house stands through the storm, while the one who does not builds on the sand and his house falls. Matthew then closes the Sermon with the crowds’ astonishment, because Jesus taught as one having authority and not as the scribes.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Jesus did not give the Sermon on the Mount only to be admired. He ends it by measuring every hearer against His own words, and the house that stands belongs to the one who hears and does them (7:24–27). The warning in 7:21–23 is spoken to people who call Jesus Lord, and it shows that ministry claims cannot take the place of obedience to the Father. Elsewhere Scripture makes clear that such obedience grows from God’s grace and the new heart He gives (Ezekiel 36:26–27; Ephesians 2:8–10).

The chapter also holds the demand and the comfort together. The same Jesus who calls His hearers to the narrow way assures His disciples that their Father gives good things to those who ask (7:11), so the obedience He asks for is lived in dependence on a generous Father.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Self-examination before correction (7:1–5). Jesus does not stop disciples from helping a brother with his fault, but He requires them to deal honestly with their own sin first.

The Father’s goodness (7:7–11). Confident prayer rests on a Father who knows how to give good things, far better than the best earthly father.

Appearance and reality (7:15–23). False prophets look like sheep, and some who say “Lord, Lord” were never known by Jesus. Fruit and obedience reveal what appearances hide.

Hearing and doing (7:21, 24–27). Both builders hear the same words. The difference lies in whether they put Jesus’ sayings into practice.

Jesus’ authority (7:22–24, 28–29). Jesus speaks as the One who will give the verdict on that day, and He makes His own sayings the foundation of life.

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Plank and speck (7:3–5). Jesus contrasts a large beam of wood with a tiny particle in someone’s eye. The exaggeration shows how easily we notice another person’s small fault while missing our own far greater one.

The Law and the Prophets (7:12). This phrase names the Hebrew Scriptures as a whole. Jesus used it earlier when He said He came to fulfill them (5:17), and here He sums up what they require in how people treat one another.

False prophets (7:15). These are people who claim to speak for God but do not. Jesus tells His disciples to recognize them by their fruit, not by their appearance.

Fruit (7:16–20). Fruit is what a life produces, especially its teaching and conduct. John the Baptist used the same picture when he called for fruit worthy of repentance (3:8–10).

That day (7:22). This expression refers to the day of judgment, when Jesus Himself will give the verdict on those who claim to belong to Him.

Scribes (7:29). The scribes were teachers who studied and explained the Law of Moses. Jesus did not teach as they did, but spoke on His own authority, as His repeated “But I say to you” shows (5:22, 28).

focus: Matthew 7 brings the Sermon on the Mount to its close as Jesus teaches His disciples to examine themselves before correcting a brother, to use discernment with what is holy, to ask confidently of their good Father, and to do for others what they would want done for them. He then presses every hearer toward a decision through contrasting gates, trees, claims, and builders, and Matthew closes the Sermon by recording the crowds’ astonishment at His authority.

sections.title: Judging Others and Exercising Discernment
sections.summary: Jesus forbids hypocritical judgment, warning that the measure we use will be measured back to us, and tells the hypocrite to remove the plank from his own eye first so that he can see clearly to remove the speck from his brother’s eye. He then warns against giving what is holy to the dogs or casting pearls before swine, since what is holy and precious may be trampled underfoot and the one who offers it may be torn in pieces.

sections.title: Ask, Seek, Knock, and the Golden Rule
sections.summary: Jesus invites His hearers to ask, seek, and knock, assuring them that if earthly fathers know how to give good gifts to their children, their Father in heaven will much more give good things to those who ask Him. He then calls them to do to others whatever they want others to do to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets.

sections.title: The Narrow and Wide Gates
sections.summary: Jesus urges His hearers to enter by the narrow gate. The wide gate and broad way lead to destruction and many go in by it, while the narrow gate and difficult way lead to life and few find it.

sections.title: Recognizing False Prophets by Their Fruit
sections.summary: Jesus warns against false prophets who come in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. As a tree is known by the fruit it bears, His disciples will know these prophets by their fruits, and every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.

sections.title: Doing the Father’s Will
sections.summary: Jesus declares that not everyone who calls Him “Lord, Lord” will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of His Father in heaven. On that day many will claim to have prophesied, cast out demons, and done many wonders in His name, yet He will declare to them, “I never knew you,” and send them away as those who practice lawlessness.

sections.title: The Wise and Foolish Builders
sections.summary: Jesus compares the one who hears His sayings and does them to a wise man whose house on the rock stands through rain, floods, and wind, and the one who hears but does not do them to a foolish man whose house on the sand falls. Matthew then closes the Sermon by recording that the people were astonished at His teaching, for He taught as one having authority and not as the scribes.

1.brief: Jesus commands His disciples, “Judge not, that you be not judged.” He warns against condemning another person while excusing our own faults, and He reminds the one who judges this way that he too will face judgment. He does not forbid every kind of evaluation, since He soon requires discernment about what is holy and about false prophets.
1.explain:
Matthew 7 brings the Sermon on the Mount to its close. In chapter 6 Jesus taught His disciples to live before their Father in secret and to trust Him instead of worrying. Now He turns to how they treat other people, beginning with a sin that religious people fall into easily: sitting in judgment over those around them.

Judge not is a command addressed to Jesus’ disciples. The word “judge” can mean anything from evaluating something to condemning someone, so the context has to show which Jesus means. He is not forbidding moral discernment. In this same chapter He tells His disciples to use discernment with what is holy (v. 6) and to recognize false prophets by their fruit (vv. 15–20). What He forbids is the condemning spirit that looks down on others, pronounces verdicts that belong to God, and excuses in ourselves what it condemns in someone else. Verses 3–5 show that this spirit is usually blind to its own faults.

that you be not judged gives the reason. The person who takes the judge’s seat over others does not escape judgment himself. He will stand before God, and the next verse explains that the way he has judged others will matter when he does. Jesus is not denying that there is right and wrong. He is warning the one who judges that he too is accountable.
1.notes:
The Greek verb translated “judge” (krinō) covers a wide range of meaning, from evaluating to condemning. Paul uses it for the church’s proper evaluation of its own members (1 Corinthians 5:12) and for condemning others (Romans 2:1; 14:13). Luke’s parallel sets the saying beside “Condemn not, and you shall not be condemned” (Luke 6:37), which supports the reading that Jesus has condemnation in view.

In the words “that you be not judged,” Jesus does not say who will do the judging. The context of final accountability points to God as the Judge. Jesus uses the same kind of wording in the Beatitudes, where God is plainly the One who acts: “they shall be comforted” (5:4) and “they shall be filled” (5:6).

2.brief: Jesus gives the reason for His command: the standard a person uses in judging others is the standard that will be applied to him. Whoever measures others severely invites the same measure in return.
2.explain:
For with what judgment you judge, you will be judged explains the command of verse 1. The judgment a person passes on others becomes the standard applied to him. Someone who condemns harshly and makes no allowance for weakness cannot expect to be treated more gently than he treats others. Paul makes the same point: “in whatever you judge another you condemn yourself” (Romans 2:1).

and with the measure you use, it will be measured back to you repeats the warning with a picture from the marketplace, where grain and other goods were measured out in containers. The measure a person uses on others is the measure that comes back to him. The verse echoes what Jesus has already taught: “Blessed are the merciful, For they shall obtain mercy” (5:7). In the Lord’s Prayer He also tied the Father’s forgiveness of us to our forgiveness of others (6:12, 14–15).
2.notes:
The Mishnah, a collection of Jewish teaching written down around AD 200, records a similar saying: the measure a man uses is the measure used for him (Sotah 1:7). The Mishnah is later than the Gospels, so the parallel shows a similar way of speaking, not where Jesus’ saying came from.

Luke’s parallel shows the generous side of the same principle. A generous measure returns “pressed down, shaken together, and running over” (Luke 6:38).

3.brief: With a deliberately exaggerated picture, Jesus asks why someone looks at the speck in his brother’s eye but does not consider the plank in his own. The question exposes how readily we magnify another person’s small fault while ignoring our own far greater one.
3.explain:
And why do you look at the speck in your brother’s eye opens a deliberately exaggerated picture. A “speck” is a tiny bit of straw, chaff, or wood, the kind of thing that blows into someone’s eye. The person Jesus describes notices it quickly and keeps his attention on it. The word “brother” shows that Jesus is speaking about relationships among God’s people, the very people we see most closely and are most tempted to examine.

but do not consider the plank in your own eye? completes the picture. A plank is a beam, the kind of heavy timber used in building. The scene is meant to be absurd: a man with a beam in his eye studying a speck in someone else’s. To “consider” is to notice and think carefully about something. The critic studies his brother’s small fault in detail and does not even notice his own far larger one. Jesus does not say the speck is imaginary. The brother has a real fault. The problem is the critic’s blindness about himself.
3.notes:
The Greek word behind “speck” (karphos) describes a small dry particle, such as a bit of straw or wood. The word behind “plank” (dokos) is the word for a large beam of timber, which shows how great the contrast is meant to be.

A later rabbinic text records a similar exchange. When one person tells another to remove a small splinter from his eye, the reply is to remove the beam from his own (Babylonian Talmud, Arakhin 16b, paraphrased). The Talmud was compiled centuries after Jesus, so this shows a similar image, not how widely the saying was known in His day.

4.brief: Jesus presses the absurdity further by picturing a man with a plank in his own eye offering to remove the speck from his brother’s eye. Help offered from such blindness is presumptuous, however kindly it is worded.
4.explain:
Or how can you say to your brother, ‘Let me remove the speck from your eye’ moves from noticing to acting. The critic’s words sound kind. He presents himself as someone who wants to help. Jesus’ question is not whether the speck should come out, but whether this person is in any condition to remove it.

and look, a plank is in your own eye? calls attention back to the scene. The man leaning in to do delicate work on his brother’s eye has a beam sticking out of his own. He cannot see well enough to help, and his efforts are more likely to injure than to heal. Correction offered while one’s own sin goes unrecognized is presumptuous, however gently it is worded.

5.brief: Jesus names this person a hypocrite and gives the right order: first remove the plank from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye. Honest self-examination comes first, and it clears the way for genuine help to a brother.
5.explain:
Hypocrite! is a sharp word, and Jesus uses it deliberately. He has already used it for those who give, pray, and fast to be seen by others (6:2, 5, 16). Here the hypocrite acts the part of the righteous helper. He shows great concern for his brother’s small fault while overlooking a far greater sin in himself.

First remove the plank from your own eye sets the order. Jesus does not tell His disciples to ignore sin in others. He tells them where to begin. Facing one’s own sin honestly, with confession and repentance, comes before addressing anyone else’s.

and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye shows that Jesus is not forbidding all correction. He wants the speck removed. The brother’s fault is real, and love will want to help him. But only a person who has humbly faced his own sin can see clearly enough to help well. These verses do not end with “leave your brother alone.” They end with a brother helped by someone who has first been humbled. Paul gives the same order when he tells spiritual believers to restore the fallen “in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself lest you also be tempted” (Galatians 6:1).
5.notes:
The word “hypocrite” returns repeatedly in Jesus’ woes against the scribes and Pharisees in chapter 23, where the charge is an outward show of righteousness that hides an inward condition (23:27–28).

Jesus later gives practical steps for going to a brother who sins (18:15–17), which shows that the correction allowed in 7:5 is real correction, not only private self-examination.

6.brief: Jesus warns against giving what is holy to the dogs or casting pearls before swine. What is holy and precious may be trampled underfoot, and the person who offers it may be attacked, so alongside humble correction He requires discernment about offering holy things to those who meet them with contempt.
6.explain:
Verse 6 balances verses 1–5. Disciples must not condemn others, but they must not be naive either. Refusing to judge harshly does not mean refusing to discern.

Do not give what is holy to the dogs uses a shocking picture. “What is holy” is something set apart to God. The Law guarded such things carefully. For example, holy food reserved for the priests was not to be eaten by an outsider (Leviticus 22:10). Against that background, throwing something set apart to God to dogs would have been unthinkable. Jesus uses the picture without saying exactly what the holy thing is. The dogs in view are not household pets but the scavengers that roamed the streets and refuse heaps of ancient towns.

nor cast your pearls before swine adds a second picture. Pearls were among the most valuable possessions in the ancient world. Jesus later compares the kingdom of heaven to a pearl worth everything a merchant owned (13:45–46). Pigs were unclean under the Law (Leviticus 11:7), and a pig sees no value in a pearl.

lest they trample them under their feet, and turn and tear you in pieces names two dangers. What is holy and precious may be treated with contempt, and the person who offers it may be attacked. Jesus does not say exactly what the holy things and pearls are. In light of verses 1–5, wise correction is a natural application. The kingdom message itself is another reasonable application, especially since Jesus later tells His disciples to shake the dust off their feet when a town refuses to receive them (10:14). Either way, the verse calls for discernment about offering holy things to people who meet them with contempt. It does not label any group of people as dogs or swine, and it does not treat honest questions as contempt. Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners (9:10–13) and sends His disciples to all nations (28:19).
6.notes:
Some interpreters see a crossed pattern in the verse, with the swine trampling the pearls and the dogs turning to attack. Others think the swine do both. The text does not settle the question, and the warning is the same either way.

Proverbs gives similar counsel about speaking to those who mock: “Do not correct a scoffer, lest he hate you” (Proverbs 9:8).

7.brief: Jesus invites His disciples to ask, seek, and knock, and He attaches a promise to each: it will be given, they will find, and it will be opened to them. The threefold invitation urges earnest and persevering prayer to the Father.
7.explain:
Jesus now turns to prayer. He does not state a link with verses 1–6, but the connection fits. Disciples who need clear sight to help a brother (v. 5) and wisdom to know when to hold back holy things (v. 6) will soon find they lack what they need. Jesus invites them to ask their Father.

Ask, and it will be given to you is the simplest form of prayer: a request made to someone able to give. The giver is not named here, but verse 11 names Him. It is the Father who gives.

seek, and you will find adds desire and effort. Jesus has already told His disciples what to seek first: “the kingdom of God and His righteousness” (6:33). The Old Testament promises that those who seek God with all their heart will find Him (Deuteronomy 4:29; Jeremiah 29:13).

knock, and it will be opened to you pictures someone standing at a closed door and asking to be let in. Each of the three commands comes with a promise, and together they describe earnest, active prayer. In Luke the same saying follows a parable about persistence in asking (Luke 11:5–10), so persevering prayer is a fitting application of these invitations.
7.notes:
In Greek all three commands are in the present tense, a form that can describe ongoing or repeated action. Many interpreters hear them as “keep on asking,” and the NLT renders them, “Keep on asking … Keep on seeking … Keep on knocking.” The form allows this reading but does not require it by itself.

In Luke this saying follows a parable about a man who goes to a friend at midnight to ask for bread. Though the friend will not get up because of friendship, Jesus says that “because of his persistence he will rise and give him as many as he needs” (Luke 11:8).

8.brief: Jesus widens the promise to include everyone who prays this way: everyone who asks receives, he who seeks finds, and to him who knocks it will be opened. No disciple who comes to the Father asking, seeking, and knocking is left out.
8.explain:
For everyone who asks receives gives the reason disciples can take up the invitations of verse 7 with confidence. Verse 7 gave commands; verse 8 gives assurance. “Everyone” is the important word. Answered prayer is not reserved for prophets, priests, or especially devout people. The promise belongs to all who come to the Father this way.

and he who seeks finds, and to him who knocks it will be opened repeats the other two actions as sure statements. The repetition is meant to reassure. The word “finds” will appear again in verse 14, where only a few find the way that leads to life.

9.brief: Jesus appeals to ordinary fatherhood by asking what man among His hearers would give his son a stone when the boy asks for bread. The question draws on the care a father normally shows, meeting his son’s need with real food rather than something useless.
9.explain:
Or what man is there among you who turns to His hearers’ own experience as fathers. Jesus invites them to think about how they treat their own children.

if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone? presents a situation every listener can picture. Bread was the basic food of daily life. A father who answered his hungry son’s request with a stone would be meeting a real need with something useless. The question appeals to the care fathers normally show, and it expects the answer no.

10.brief: Jesus adds a second example, asking whether a father would give his son a serpent when he asks for a fish. This example goes further than the first by picturing a gift that is not merely useless but harmful, and both questions prepare for Jesus’ comparison with the Father in heaven.
10.explain: Or if he asks for a fish, will he give him a serpent? adds a second example that goes further than the first. Fish was a common food in Galilee and was often eaten with bread (14:17). A serpent is not only useless as food but dangerous. The first question pictured a gift that would not help. This one pictures a gift that would harm. Again the expected answer is no, and both questions prepare for the comparison with the Father in the next verse.

11.brief: Jesus reasons from the lesser to the greater: if His hearers, being evil, know how to give good gifts to their children, how much more will their Father in heaven give good things to those who ask Him. The disciple’s confidence in prayer rests on the Father’s goodness and on His wisdom in giving what is truly good.
11.explain:
If you then, being evil states plainly that His hearers are sinful. Jesus does not mean that every human act is wicked, since He goes on to say they give good gifts. He means that human nature is fallen, and even the best father is not good the way God is good.

know how to give good gifts to your children acknowledges that even sinful parents know how to give their children what they need. Love for one’s children survives in fallen people.

how much more will your Father who is in heaven is the heart of Jesus’ argument. If imperfect fathers give good gifts, the Father whose goodness has no flaw will give far more. Throughout the sermon Jesus has spoken of God as the disciples’ Father in heaven (5:16, 45; 6:1, 9). His disciples come to God as children come to a father.

give good things to those who ask Him! promises that the Father gives what is truly good. He is wiser than we are about what is good, so He may not give everything in the form we ask for it. But He does not answer His children with harm in place of good. “Those who ask Him” ties the promise back to verse 7.
11.notes:
Jesus reasons from the lesser to the greater. Even imperfect fathers give good gifts to their children, so disciples can be all the more confident in the goodness of their Father in heaven. He uses the same kind of reasoning for God’s care in 6:30 (“will He not much more clothe you”) and for the value of a person in 12:12.

Luke’s parallel has “give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him” where Matthew has “good things” (Luke 11:13).

12.brief: Jesus draws a conclusion with “Therefore”: whatever you want men to do to you, do also to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets. Following His teaching on the Father’s generosity, Jesus calls disciples to take the initiative in treating others as they would want to be treated, and He presents this as the sum of what the Law and the Prophets require in how people treat one another.
12.explain:
Therefore ties this command to what comes before. The most likely immediate link is the Father’s goodness in verses 7–11: those who receive good things from the Father are to do good to others. The verse also gathers up the sermon’s teaching on how disciples are to treat other people.

whatever you want men to do to you, do also to them is positive and active. Jesus does not simply say, “Do not harm others.” He tells His disciples to think about what they would want from others, such as patience, honesty, mercy, fairness, and help in a time of need, and then to take the first step in giving it. The command does not wait for others to treat us well first. It calls for love even when kindness is not returned.

for this is the Law and the Prophets explains why the command matters so much. “The Law and the Prophets” means the Old Testament Scriptures. At the start of His teaching on the Law, Jesus said He did not come to destroy the Law or the Prophets but “to fulfill” them (5:17). Here He sums up what they require in how people treat one another. Later He says that all the Law and the Prophets hang on loving God and loving one’s neighbor as oneself (22:37–40).
12.notes:
Similar sayings existed in Jewish tradition, usually in a negative form. Tobit 4:15, written before Jesus’ time, says not to do to anyone what you hate. The Babylonian Talmud (Shabbat 31a), compiled centuries later, attributes a comparable saying to Hillel, a teacher of the generation before Jesus. Matthew records the positive form.

The sermon refers to “the Law or the Prophets” in 5:17 and to “the Law and the Prophets” here in 7:12. These two references frame the main body of the sermon. What follows in 7:13–27 is the conclusion, a series of contrasts that call for a decision.

13.brief: Jesus commands, “Enter by the narrow gate,” and warns that the gate is wide and the way broad that leads to destruction, with many going in by it. The easy and crowded way ends in ruin, so no one should take it simply because many others do.
13.explain:
With verse 13 the sermon moves into its conclusion. From here to the end, Jesus sets pairs before His hearers: two gates and two ways (vv. 13–14), good and bad trees (vv. 15–20), those who only say “Lord, Lord” and those who do the Father’s will (vv. 21–23), and two builders (vv. 24–27). Each pair calls for a decision.

Enter by the narrow gate is a command. Jesus has described life in the kingdom of heaven, and now He calls His hearers to enter it. A gate is the way into a city or a walled place, and verse 14 shows that this gate leads to life. Each hearer is called to enter personally.

for wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction describes the other option. The gate is wide and the road broad, and verse 14 sets them against a narrow gate and a difficult way. Jesus does not describe the journey in detail. What matters is where the broad way leads. Its end is “destruction,” the final ruin that stands opposite to “life” in verse 14.

and there are many who go in by it warns that the broad way is crowded. The number of travelers can make it feel safe, but the crowd does not change where the road ends. No one should take it simply because many others do.
13.notes: The Greek word for “destruction” (apōleia) is used elsewhere in the New Testament for the final ruin of those who oppose God (Philippians 1:28; 3:19; 2 Peter 3:7).

14.brief: Jesus explains why the narrow gate must be entered: it and the difficult way lead to life, and there are few who find it. The way of life under Jesus’ teaching is demanding, and the contrast between the few and the many presses each hearer to enter that gate.
14.explain:
Because narrow is the gate and difficult is the way which leads to life explains why the narrow gate must be entered. The way beyond it is “difficult,” a word that means pressed or confined. Those who walk this way meet opposition and the cost of following Jesus, as He has already said (5:10–12) and will say again: “If anyone desires to come after Me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow Me” (16:24). The narrow way takes shape in living under Jesus’ authority even when obedience is hard. But it leads to “life,” which in Matthew is the life of God’s kingdom, eternal life (19:16–17, 29; 25:46).

and there are few who find it completes the contrast with the many of verse 13. “Find” recalls the promise of verse 8: “he who seeks finds.” Jesus is not giving a count of the saved or a forecast of numbers. He is warning each hearer not to assume that following the majority will bring him to life. When someone once asked Him, “Lord, are there few who are saved?” He answered, “Strive to enter through the narrow gate” (Luke 13:23–24). The question of how many becomes the question of whether you will enter.
14.notes:
The Greek verb behind “difficult” (thlibō) means to press, crowd, or confine, so the way is pictured as pressed in. The related Greek noun thlipsis is translated “tribulation” in Matthew 13:21 and 24:9, 21, 29.

The NKJV reads “Because narrow is the gate,” following Greek manuscripts that have the word for “because” here. Other Greek manuscripts have a word that can mean “how,” which turns the line into an exclamation. Young’s Literal Translation renders it “how strait [is] the gate.” The warning is the same either way.

15.brief: Jesus warns His disciples to beware of false prophets, who come to them in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. They look as though they belong to the flock, yet like wolves among sheep they are a danger to it.
15.explain:
Having called His hearers to the narrow way, Jesus warns them about people who would lead them away from it.

Beware of false prophets calls disciples to be on guard. A false prophet claims to speak for God when God has not sent him (Jeremiah 14:14; 23:16, 21), or leads people away from the LORD (Deuteronomy 13:1–5). Israel’s history was full of such voices, often promising peace without repentance: “Saying, ‘Peace, peace!’ When there is no peace” (Jeremiah 6:14). Jesus warns that false prophets will continue to arise (24:11, 24).

who come to you in sheep’s clothing describes how they appear. They look like sheep. They seem to belong to the flock, speak its language, and share its practices. They “come to you,” moving among God’s people. Their danger lies in how closely they resemble the real thing.

but inwardly they are ravenous wolves reveals what they are underneath. A wolf among sheep is a danger to the flock, and “ravenous” pictures one that snatches and devours. Whatever such prophets seem to offer, the flock is harmed by them. Paul used the same picture when he warned the Ephesian elders that “savage wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock” (Acts 20:29).

This warning does not make all prophetic ministry suspect. Elsewhere believers are told, “Do not despise prophecies. Test all things; hold fast what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21). Jesus warns against false prophets because true prophecy is real and valuable.
15.notes:
Some interpreters see an allusion to the rough garment that marked a prophet (2 Kings 1:8; Matthew 3:4), which false prophets also wore to deceive (Zechariah 13:4). The contrast with wolves, however, suggests the simpler picture: they look like members of the flock.

The Greek word for “ravenous” (harpax) is related to the verb used in John 10:12, where the wolf “catches” the sheep. It describes greedy seizing.

16.brief: Jesus gives the test, “You will know them by their fruits,” and asks whether men gather grapes from thornbushes or figs from thistles. Just as a plant is known by what it yields, a prophet’s teaching and conduct are the fruit that reveal what he truly is.
16.explain:
You will know them by their fruits gives the disciples a practical test. A false prophet’s appearance may deceive, but his fruit shows what he is. The fruit is what a prophet’s own teaching and conduct reveal: what he says, how he lives, and the character his words and life display (12:33–37). Jesus tells His disciples to examine that evidence.

Do men gather grapes from thornbushes or figs from thistles? is meant to sound ridiculous. Grapes and figs were the prized fruits of Israel (Micah 4:4). Thornbushes and thistles were weeds. No one goes to a thornbush expecting grapes. A plant is known by what it yields.
16.notes: The Greek words for thorns and thistles also occur together in the Greek translation of Genesis 3:18.

17.brief: Jesus states the principle that every good tree bears good fruit, but a bad tree bears bad fruit. The quality of a tree shows itself in the fruit it bears.
17.explain:
Even so, every good tree bears good fruit applies the picture of verse 16. A good tree is healthy and sound, and its fruit is good because of what the tree is.

but a bad tree bears bad fruit states the other side. The word translated “bad” can mean rotten or worthless. In Jesus’ picture, tree and fruit match: a good tree yields good fruit, and a bad tree yields bad fruit. The quality of the tree shows itself in what it bears.
17.notes: Matthew uses the same Greek word for “bad” (sapros) again for bad trees and fruit (12:33) and for the worthless fish thrown away from the net (13:48). Paul uses it for “corrupt” speech (Ephesians 4:29).

18.brief: Jesus makes the principle firm: a good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a bad tree bear good fruit. Good fruit does not fit a bad tree, nor bad fruit a good one, so a prophet’s fruit, not his appearance, is the evidence disciples are to examine.
18.explain: A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a bad tree bear good fruit moves from what trees do (v. 17) to what they cannot do. Good fruit does not fit a bad tree, and bad fruit does not fit a good one. Jesus is describing the settled pattern of a life, not a single act. A good person can sin, and a bad person can do something kind. Yet one serious harm, when it comes to light, can itself be weighty evidence, and disciples need not wait for repeated damage before taking it seriously. The point of the image is that a prophet’s fruit, not his appearance, is the evidence disciples are to weigh. Jesus gives them that evidence without promising how soon deception will come to light.
18.notes: Matthew 12:33 repeats the saying that a tree is known by its fruit, there applied to the Pharisees’ words about Jesus.

19.brief: Jesus warns that every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. The image echoes John the Baptist’s warning in Matthew 3:10 and shows that a life without good fruit faces God’s judgment.
19.explain:
Every tree that does not bear good fruit widens the warning. Jesus speaks of trees that fail to bear good fruit, not only trees that bear bad fruit.

is cut down and thrown into the fire repeats almost exactly the words of John the Baptist: “every tree which does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire” (3:10). Jesus confirms John’s warning. In Matthew, fire pictures God’s final judgment (3:12; 13:42; 25:41). For John the good fruit was the fruit of repentance (3:8), and a life without that fruit faces God’s judgment.
19.notes:
The words “is cut down and thrown into the fire” match the closing words of Matthew 3:10 exactly in Greek.

“Is cut down” is in the present tense in Greek. Here it states a general truth about what happens to a fruitless tree, not a particular moment.

20.brief: Jesus repeats the conclusion, “Therefore by their fruits you will know them.” The repetition closes the section and fixes the test His disciples are to use in recognizing false prophets.
20.explain: Therefore by their fruits you will know them draws the conclusion from the images of trees and fruit. The sentence repeats verse 16 almost word for word, framing the whole section and fixing the test in the disciples’ minds. They are not left defenseless against deception. They have a test Jesus Himself gave for recognizing false prophets.

21.brief: Jesus declares that not everyone who says to Him, “Lord, Lord,” shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of His Father in heaven. Speaking as the Son who calls God “My Father,” Jesus makes obedience to the Father’s will, and not words of devotion alone, the mark of those who enter the kingdom.
21.explain:
Jesus moves from false prophets to a wider warning addressed to everyone who claims to follow Him. For the first time in the sermon He also speaks of His own role at the final judgment.

Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ describes people who address Jesus as Lord. In this setting the title means far more than polite respect. These people speak to Jesus as the One with authority over their eternal destiny. The doubled “Lord, Lord” expresses earnestness and familiarity. They speak as people who know Him and confess Him openly.

shall enter the kingdom of heaven refers to entering God’s kingdom in its final, complete form (5:20; 18:3; 19:23–24). Jesus has just called His hearers to enter by the narrow gate (v. 13). Now He shows that some who appear to be on the way will not enter.

but he who does the will of My Father in heaven names the one who enters. Jesus has spent three chapters describing the Father’s will: a righteousness from the heart that goes beyond outward religion (5:20). Words of devotion without that obedience are empty. Jesus also calls God “My Father.” He has spoken of “your Father” and taught His disciples to pray “Our Father” (6:9). Here, for the first time in Matthew, He speaks of God as His own Father. The One who will stand as Judge is the Son.

This obedience does not earn the kingdom. The wider New Testament teaches that we are saved by grace through faith and created in Christ Jesus “for good works” (Ephesians 2:8–10), and the prophets promised that God would put His Spirit within His people and cause them to walk in His ways (Ezekiel 36:26–27). Jesus’ point here is that a life of obedience shows real allegiance to Him. A profession without it does not.
21.notes: Luke records the same concern as a pointed question: “But why do you call Me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do the things which I say?” (Luke 6:46).

22.brief: Jesus foresees that “in that day” many will say to Him, “Lord, Lord,” and appeal to having prophesied, cast out demons, and done many wonders in His name. Jesus Himself is the One they will face on the day of judgment, and their appeal rests on ministry claims that the verse reports without confirming.
22.explain:
Many will say to Me in that day continues the scene. “Many” is a sobering word. Jesus is not describing a rare exception. “That day” is the day of judgment (24:36), and Jesus presents Himself as the One before whom people will stand and give account (25:31–32). A teacher on a hillside in Galilee is claiming the role the Old Testament gives to God Himself.

Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in Your name begins their appeal to ministry. First they mention prophecy. That connects naturally with the false prophets of verse 15, but the warning of verses 21–23 is broader. It concerns everyone who professes Jesus as Lord. To prophesy “in Your name” means to speak claiming Jesus’ authority.

cast out demons in Your name, and done many wonders in Your name? completes the list with deliverance from demons and many miracles. Three times they say “in Your name.” These are the kinds of works Jesus later gives His disciples authority to do (10:1, 8). The verse reports their claims. It does not say whether the works really happened or what power was behind them. Verse 23 shows that their appeal to ministry cannot stand in place of the relationship they lacked.
22.notes: In Greek the phrase translated “in Your name” comes before the verb in each of the three clauses, so the speakers stress Jesus’ name each time. An explanatory rendering would be: in Your name we prophesied, in Your name we cast out demons, in Your name we did many mighty works. “Wonders” translates the Greek word dunameis, the usual word for Jesus’ mighty works (11:20–23; 13:54).

23.brief: Jesus will then declare to them, “I never knew you,” and command them to depart from Him as those who practice lawlessness. His verdict exposes that they never had the relationship with Him they presumed, and their lawless way of life contradicts their profession.
23.explain:
And then I will declare to them introduces Jesus’ verdict. To “declare” is to state openly. The same verb appears in 10:32, where Jesus promises to “confess” before His Father those who confess Him. Here it introduces a solemn public verdict.

I never knew you does not mean that Jesus was unaware of these people or of what they claimed. In Scripture “know” often describes a committed personal relationship. The LORD said to Israel, “You only have I known of all the families of the earth” (Amos 3:2), and Jesus says, “I know My sheep, and am known by My own” (John 10:14). “Never” matters. Jesus does not say He once knew them and later stopped. Whatever ministry they claimed, the relationship they assumed was never there.

depart from Me pronounces separation from His presence, the greatest loss a person can suffer (25:41; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). It is the opposite of His invitation, “Come to Me” (11:28), and of His welcome to the righteous, “Come, you blessed of My Father” (25:34).

you who practice lawlessness! names what their lives showed. “Lawlessness” means disregard for God’s law and will. It is the opposite of doing “the will of My Father” (v. 21). These people called Jesus Lord but lived as their own lords, and their lawless way of life contradicted their profession. Jesus speaks this warning to people who profess faith in Him. The passage presses home the danger without settling every question about perseverance and assurance.
23.notes:
Jesus’ words closely follow the Greek translation of Psalm 6:8. In the NKJV the psalm reads, “Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity.” In the psalm David speaks to his enemies after the LORD has heard his prayer. Here Jesus speaks the words as Judge.

The Greek word behind “lawlessness” (anomia) appears again in Matthew for those gathered out of the kingdom at the end of the age (13:41), for the hypocrisy of the scribes and Pharisees (23:28), and for the lawlessness that will cause the love of many to grow cold (24:12).

24.brief: Jesus concludes the Sermon with “Therefore”: whoever hears “these sayings of Mine” and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock. The rock foundation pictures hearing Jesus’ teaching and putting it into practice, and that doing is what makes this hearer wise.
24.explain:
Therefore whoever hears these sayings of Mine, and does them brings the whole sermon to its point. “These sayings of Mine” are the words of the Sermon on the Mount. Jesus makes His own words the foundation of life, a role the Old Testament gives to the word of God. Hearing and doing go together. A person must hear Jesus’ words, but hearing is not enough. He must put them into practice: forgiving, praying in secret, refusing to worry, treating others as he wants to be treated. James says the same: “But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves” (James 1:22).

I will liken him to a wise man who built his house on the rock gives the picture. “Wise” here means practical good sense that acts in light of what is coming (24:45; 25:2). Matthew does not describe the builder’s plans or methods. He simply sets the house on the rock, and the parable makes that rock foundation correspond to hearing Jesus’ words and doing them. That doing is what makes this hearer wise.
24.notes: Many valleys in Israel are dry much of the year, and heavy winter rains can turn them into sudden torrents. A setting like this may lie behind the picture, though Matthew leaves the precise setting and the building methods unspecified beyond the contrast of rock and sand. The detail that the wise builder “dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock” comes from Luke’s parallel (Luke 6:48).

25.brief: The rain descends, the floods come, and the winds beat on the wise man’s house, yet it does not fall, because it was founded on the rock. The wise builder is not spared the storm, but his house stands because of what it rests on.
25.explain:
and the rain descended, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house describes a storm that comes from every direction: rain from above, floods rising from below, and wind striking from the side. The wise builder is not spared the storm. Everything beats against his house at once.

and it did not fall, for it was founded on the rock explains why the house stood. Its survival depended on what lay beneath it. The outcome was settled long before the storm arrived, on the day the foundation was laid.
25.notes: The Greek word behind “floods” is potamoi, which literally means “rivers.” In this storm scene it pictures rushing torrents of water.

26.brief: Jesus describes the other hearer: everyone who hears these sayings and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. Both men hear the same words, and the foolish man’s failure lies in not acting on them.
26.explain:
But everyone who hears these sayings of Mine, and does not do them describes the second hearer. The foolish man also hears. He sat under the same teaching and heard the same words as the wise man. He may have admired them and agreed with them. The difference is that he did not do them.

will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand gives the picture. “Foolish” in Scripture does not mean lacking intelligence. It describes a person who fails to act wisely toward God (Psalm 14:1). Matthew does not say how this man built or what he expected. He says only that he built on sand. Luke’s parallel adds that he built “without a foundation” (Luke 6:49). Until the storm came, the difference between the two houses might not have been obvious.
26.notes: The Greek adjective behind “foolish” (mōros) is also used for the unprepared virgins in Matthew 25:2–3, 8.

27.brief: The same rain, floods, and winds beat on the foolish man’s house, and it falls, “And great was its fall.” Because Jesus has just spoken of “that day,” the collapse most likely points to the ruin that final judgment will expose, though present trials can also reveal what a life is built on.
27.explain:
and the rain descended, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house repeats the NKJV wording of verse 25 exactly. Both houses face the same storm.

and it fell states the outcome. The house on the rock “did not fall” (v. 25), but this house fell. Jesus has already named what made the difference: one man did what he heard, and the other did not (vv. 24, 26).

And great was its fall closes the sermon. The collapse was complete. Coming right after Jesus’ words about “that day” (v. 22), the storm most likely points especially to the final judgment, when the difference between hearing and doing will be fully exposed. In the Old Testament, judgment is often pictured as a destroying storm and flood (Isaiah 28:17; Ezekiel 13:11–13). The trials of this life can also reveal what a life is built on, but the sermon ends on the warning of final ruin for those who hear Jesus’ words and do not do them.
27.notes: The Greek verbs for the storm striking the houses differ slightly. In verse 25 the storm falls against the house (prospiptō), and in verse 27 it strikes against the house (proskoptō). The two verbs are close in meaning, and the NKJV renders both “beat on.”

28.brief: Matthew records that when Jesus had ended these sayings, the people were astonished at His teaching. The account now steps back from Jesus’ words and closes the Sermon on the Mount with the crowd’s response.
28.explain:
And so it was, when Jesus had ended these sayings marks the end of the Sermon on the Mount. Matthew uses a similar formula at the close of each of Jesus’ five major teaching sections (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1). The narrative now steps back from Jesus’ words to the response of His hearers.

that the people were astonished at His teaching describes that response. “The people” are the crowds who had followed Jesus from Galilee and beyond (4:25; 5:1). The sermon was addressed to His disciples (5:1–2), but the crowds heard it too. “Astonished” means overwhelmed with amazement. Verse 29 explains why.
28.notes: The Greek verb for “astonished” (ekplēssō) means to be struck with amazement. Matthew uses it for the reaction at Nazareth (13:54), for the disciples’ shock at Jesus’ words about riches (19:25), and for the crowd’s response to His answer about the resurrection (22:33).

29.brief: Matthew explains their astonishment: Jesus taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes. Throughout the Sermon He had spoken on His own authority, as His repeated “But I say to you” shows (Matthew 5:22, 28), and the crowds recognized the difference.
29.explain:
for He taught them as one having authority explains the crowd’s amazement. “Authority” means both the right and the power to act. Throughout the sermon Jesus spoke on His own authority: “But I say to you” (5:22, 28, 32, 34, 39, 44). He gave the true meaning of God’s Law, made His own words the foundation of life (v. 24), and presented Himself as the Judge on the last day (vv. 21–23). The chapters that follow show the same authority over disease (8:1–17), storms (8:23–27), demons (8:28–34), and sin (9:6).

and not as the scribes draws the contrast. The scribes were experts in the Law of Moses and were respected for their learning. Matthew does not describe how they taught in this scene. The contrast centers on Jesus. He spoke on His own authority, as the One with the right to declare God’s will, and the crowds recognized the difference.
29.notes:
Greek manuscripts differ over whether a possessive pronoun meaning “their” is present with “scribes.” In the Greek reading that includes it, the pronoun follows the word for “scribes.” The NKJV, following manuscripts without it, reads “the scribes,” while the ESV and NASB, following the reading with it, have “their scribes.” Matthew often uses “their” in similar phrases, such as “their synagogues” (4:23; 9:35).

Mark records the same reaction to Jesus’ teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum (Mark 1:22).
